extraction.name: OpenBookQA
extraction.description: A new kind of question answering dataset modeled after open book exams for assessing human understanding of elementary level science. The dataset consists of 5957 multiple-choice questions that probe understanding of 1326 elementary science facts and their application to novel situations, requiring combining an open book fact with broad common knowledge.
extraction.creator: Todor Mihaylov, Peter Clark, Tushar Khot, Ashish Sabharwal
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Multi-stage crowdsourcing process starting with a set of 1326 core science facts from WorldTree corpus. Crowd-workers were shown a random science fact and asked to think of a second common fact that may be combined with the core fact to derive a new valid assertion, then convert this into a question-answer pair and extend it into a 4-way multiple choice question by adding 3 incorrect answer choices.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The core facts (F) consist of 1326 facts taken from the WorldTree corpus, specifically from 2287 WorldTree facts that were marked as 'central' by the original authors in at least one explanation, further filtered to those that appear general enough to be applicable to multiple situations.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The answer choices of questions were randomly shuffled to avoid unintended bias. At the end of Step 4, choice 'A' was the correct answer in 69% of the questions, which was corrected through shuffling.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Basic checks were performed including: 1) exactly 4 answer choices; 2) no negation words to trivially fool baselines (no, none, not, isn't, doesn't, aren't, don't, won't, except, can't, shouldn't, wouldn't, couldn't, mustn't); 3) uniform answer choice length: all with at most 3 or at least 4 words. Questions were verified to be hard for an information retrieval solver and a word association based solver. Dev and Test splits were further filtered by an in-house expert to ensure higher quality.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Crowd-workers created questions by: 1) viewing a random science fact from F; 2) thinking of a second common fact k that may be combined with the core fact to derive a new valid assertion; 3) converting this into a question-answer pair and extending to 4-way multiple choice by adding 3 incorrect answer choices. Each question was then shown to 5 new crowd-workers who were asked to answer it. If at least 4 out of 5 workers answered correctly, it was deemed answerable and kept in the dataset.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Questions were verified for answerability: if at least 4 out of 5 workers answered a question correctly, it was deemed answerable and the process continued. If not, the question was discarded. Human accuracy was estimated using a Bernoulli random variable model with 5 independent samples per question.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Workers from North America with a 'masters' level qualification on Amazon Mechanical Turk
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Analysis revealed inevitable human bias in the crowdsourced dataset. The plausible answer detector baseline (which ignores the question text completely) achieved 49.6% accuracy, and the odd-one-out solver achieved 50.2%, highlighting bias arising from the fact that creating good quality incorrect answers is difficult. Workers generally start with the correct answer and then come up with three incorrect ones, which often tend to be homogeneous or share other common properties uncharacteristic of the correct answer. Choice 'A' was the correct answer in 69% of questions before shuffling.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset has several limitations: (a) In 21% of analyzed cases, the crowdsourced question actually tests for a fact that doesn't necessarily need the original science fact; (b) The second facts (K) provided by question authors are often incomplete, over-complete, or only distantly related to the questions; (c) Some questions fall outside the domain of Science where most core facts come from; (d) The dataset requires relatively simple common knowledge (taxonomic facts, definitions, object properties), but the difficulty lies in identifying it and meaningfully combining it with a core fact.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is split into Train/Dev/Test sets with 4957/500/500 questions respectively. It is designed for training and evaluating question answering systems that can combine core science facts with broad common knowledge through multi-hop reasoning. For each Train and Dev question, the dataset includes the core fact f as intermediate supervision signal, which may be viewed as a partial explanation. The dataset is intended to probe deeper understanding of both the topic in the context of common knowledge and the language it is expressed in.
